title: In Place and Inside Out
focus: Using the array as its own hash table, a stack that ranks, and flooding from the wrong end.

cards.title: Array as Hash Table
patterns: Place values at their own index
Answer lives in the first gap
cards.trigger: O(1) space demanded, and the answer is about which small positive integers are present.
cards.recall: Write it from memory. Then answer the two-part question: why can the answer only ever be in the range 1 to n+1, and what makes the swap loop terminate?
useWhen: First missing positive
Find all numbers disappeared or duplicated in an array
Set mismatch, one duplicated and one missing
Any 'values in 1..n' question with an O(1) space constraint
Where you would reach for a hash set but are not allowed one
template: # Place each value v in 1..n at index v-1
while 1 <= nums[i] <= n and nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i]:
nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]     # do NOT advance i
# Sign-marking variant, when values are guaranteed in 1..n:
# any index still positive was never seen
keyInsights: With n slots, the smallest missing positive is at most n+1. That bound is what makes constant space possible
The swap condition compares values, not indices, so duplicates do not cause an infinite loop
Every swap places at least one value correctly forever, so total swaps are bounded by n. That is the linear-time argument
cards.trap: 'Prove it is O(n) with that nested while loop.' Same amortised argument as longest-consecutive-sequence. Have it ready, they always ask.

cards.title: Maximum Frequency Stack
cards.trigger: Pop the most frequent element, breaking ties by most recent.
cards.recall: Sketch it from memory. Then answer the design insight: when you push a value for the third time, why does it get added to the frequency-3 stack while remaining in the 1 and 2 stacks?
useWhen: Maximum frequency stack
Any pop-by-count-then-recency policy
LFU-flavoured structures needing O(1) both ways
Undo systems ranked by usage
Where a heap would give log n and O(1) is required
template: self.group = defaultdict(list)    # count -> stack of values at that count
self.group[f].append(val)         # stays in groups 1..f-1 as well
self.max_freq -= 1            # only ever decreases by one
keyInsights: Leaving the value in the lower groups is what makes pop correct: after popping, its earlier occurrence is already sitting in group f-1
`max_freq` decreases by exactly one when its group empties, so no scan is ever needed
Each group is a stack, which gives the most-recent tie-break for free
cards.trap: 'What is the space complexity?' O(n) total pushes, not O(n * max_freq), because each push adds exactly one entry. Count carefully before answering.

cards.title: Collecting Root-to-Leaf Paths
patterns: Preorder with a live path list
cards.trigger: Return the actual paths, not just a count or a maximum.
cards.recall: Write path sum II from memory. Then answer the two lines people forget: which copy, and which pop, and what happens if you drop each one.
useWhen: Path sum II, all root-to-leaf paths
Binary tree paths as strings
Sum root-to-leaf numbers
Smallest string starting from a leaf
Any question asking for the paths themselves
template: if not node.left and not node.right and remaining == 0:
out.append(path[:])            # COPY, the live list keeps changing
path.pop()                          # BACKTRACK on the way out
# Leaf test is 'no left AND no right'. A node with one child is NOT a leaf,
# which is the classic off-by-one in every path problem.
keyInsights: `path[:]` copies. Without it, every recorded path is the same list object and ends up empty
The pop must be outside every branch, so it runs on the record path too. Putting it in an else is the standard bug
Complexity is O(n^2) in the worst case because each recorded path can be O(n) long. Say that, do not claim O(n)
cards.trap: 'The path can start anywhere, not just the root.' That is path sum III, which wants prefix sums with a counter map. Different problem, similar name.

cards.title: Carry Both Extremes
cards.trigger: A running optimum where a single operation can turn the worst candidate into the best.
cards.recall: Write maximum product subarray from memory. Then answer why tracking only the maximum is insufficient, with a three-element example.
useWhen: Maximum product subarray
Maximum absolute sum of a subarray
Any Kadane variant where sign or direction can flip
Best sequence under a multiplicative or alternating rule
Where the worst-so-far is a candidate for best-next
template: hi, lo = lo, hi          # a negative turns the smallest into the largest
hi = max(x, hi * x)          # extend, or restart at x
#   after -4  : swap -> hi=-6,lo=-3; hi=max(-4,24)=24   <- lo carried the answer
keyInsights: The most negative running product is a genuine candidate for the largest, one negative number later. That is why you carry both
Swap before you update, not after. Updating first uses the wrong pairing and silently gives wrong answers
Zeros reset both, and the `max(x, ...)` and `min(x, ...)` restarts handle that without a special case
cards.trap: 'What about integer overflow?' Python is fine, other languages are not. Mentioning the language-dependent caveat unprompted reads well.

cards.title: Flood from the Destination
patterns: Start from the border, walk inward
cards.trigger: 'Which cells can reach X' where running a search from every cell would be quadratic.
cards.recall: Explain the inversion before revealing: the water flows downhill to the ocean, but the DFS goes uphill from the ocean. Say why that is equivalent and why it is faster.
useWhen: Pacific Atlantic water flow
Surrounded regions, keep what touches the border
Number of enclaves, walls and gates
Any 'can reach the outside' question
Where a per-cell search would be O(cells^2)
template: if ((r, c) in seen or r < 0 or r >= rows or c < 0 or c >= cols
or heights[r][c] < prev):        # INVERTED: only go uphill
climb(r+1, c, seen, h); climb(r-1, c, seen, h)
climb(r, c+1, seen, h); climb(r, c-1, seen, h)
return [list(cell) for cell in pac & atl]     # reaches BOTH
keyInsights: Reversing the direction turns 'search from every cell' into 'search from every border cell', which visits each cell a constant number of times
The comparison flips from 'can flow down' to 'can climb up', and the equal case must be allowed in both
Two separate visited sets, intersected at the end, is the whole answer once the inversion is in place
cards.trap: 'Surrounded regions.' Same inversion: mark everything reachable from the border as safe, then flip the rest. Solving it directly, region by region, is far more code.
